nameStory: Wall screw-moss gets its name from two distinctive features: it loves growing on walls and other stone surfaces, and its leaves spiral around the stem like the threads of a screw. When you look closely at this little moss, you can see how the leaves twist and curl in a corkscrew pattern, especially when the moss dries out.
description: Wall screw-moss is a small, cushion-forming moss that creates dense, low patches on walls, rocks, and concrete surfaces. The individual plants are tiny, usually less than an inch tall, but they group together to form soft, spongy mats that can spread several inches across. This hardy little moss has a grayish-green color when dry and becomes a brighter green when wet. Its most distinctive feature is the way its narrow leaves spiral around the stem in a twisted, screw-like pattern.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, pointed leaves that spiral around the stem in a distinctive corkscrew pattern, especially noticeable when the moss is dry and the leaves curl inward

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms dense, low cushions or mats that feel soft and spongy to the touch, rarely growing more than an inch high

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found growing on human-made surfaces like concrete walls, sidewalks, brick, and stone rather than natural soil or wood

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Changes from grayish-green or silvery when dry to bright emerald green when wet, with the color change happening quickly after rain

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels crispy and brittle when dry but becomes soft and velvety when moist, with individual cushions having a firm, dense structure

habitat: Wall screw-moss is a pioneer of urban and suburban environments, thriving on concrete walls, sidewalks, brick buildings, stone steps, and mortar between stones. It's particularly common in areas with some lime or calcium, as it tolerates alkaline conditions well. You'll often find it in cities and towns rather than deep in the woods, making it one of the most urban-adapted mosses in New England.

seasonality.spring: Becomes vibrant green as spring rains arrive, with sporophytes (spore capsules) often visible as tiny reddish-brown structures on thin stalks. This is the best time to see the moss at its most colorful and active.
seasonality.summer: May appear grayish and dormant during dry spells, but quickly greens up after summer storms. The screw-like leaf pattern is most obvious when the moss is in this dried state.
seasonality.fall: Continues to be active with autumn rains, often producing new growth and sporophytes. The cushions may expand as cooler, wetter weather returns.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible but often grayish and compressed, though it can green up during winter thaws. Hardy enough to survive freezing temperatures and snow cover.

funFact: Wall screw-moss is one of nature's ultimate urban survivors – it can actually absorb water and nutrients directly from air pollution and dust, allowing it to thrive on seemingly barren concrete surfaces where no other plants can survive!
confusionNotes: Most other small mosses prefer natural surfaces like soil, rocks, or wood, while wall screw-moss almost exclusively grows on human-made materials. The distinctive spiral leaf arrangement also sets it apart – if you see a moss making perfect little screws with its leaves, you've found your wall screw-moss.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'wall' moss, this species is actually a worldwide traveler that has spread along with human construction and trade routes. It's so well-adapted to urban life that botanists sometimes call it a 'synanthropic' species – meaning it benefits from living alongside humans.
compareHints: Wall screw-moss is the only Tortula species commonly found in New England, making identification easier once you learn its key features. Compared to other small cushion mosses in the region, it's distinguished by its preference for alkaline, human-made surfaces and its distinctive spiral leaf arrangement. Most similar mosses in other families lack the pronounced screw-like leaf pattern and typically grow on natural substrates rather than concrete and mortar.
